transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it’s nice to meet you too, but honestly, I’m just... I don't even really know where to start, to be perfectly honest. I work as a mechanic, an automotive service technician, and I’ve been doing that for a while now after I did a couple years of college and realized I just wanted to work with my hands. And you have to understand, a garage is a really, really loud place. You’ve got pneumatic tools, impact wrenches going off, air compressors cycling, people yelling over the bays... so you get used to tuning out a lot of background noise. You have to, or you'd go crazy. 

But lately... I mean, what actually brought me in today is that I can't tune this out, because it's not normal shop noise. I keep hearing this voice. It’s a man’s voice, and it’s coming directly out of the garage vents. At first I thought maybe it was sound carrying from the office HVAC, but it's not. And then sometimes, I'll pull a vehicle into my bay and pop the hood, and the voice is coming from right under the hood. Like, right next to the manifold. And it’s not muffled or distant—it is as clear as somebody standing right next to me, leaning over my shoulder. 

And it’s what he’s saying that’s really messing with me. He keeps telling me not to trust my husband. Just over and over, whispering these awful things about my husband and telling me I can't trust him. And then it bleeds into my work, too, because the voice will suddenly tell me not to touch certain cars. I'll get a repair ticket for a routine brake job or a timing belt, and the man's voice will just firmly tell me not to touch that specific car, and it's so real and so clear that I just have to back away. I can't even do my job right now because of it, and I just... I don't know how he's getting in the vents, or if I'm just losing my mind, but it's every single day.
Have you used methamphetamine, cocaine, or any other recreational drugs recently?

No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I completely understand why you would ask that, I really do, because let’s be honest, automotive shops have a certain reputation, right? People think it’s all rough-around-the-edges guys and that maybe there’s people doing lines in the employee bathroom or smoking something out by the dumpsters on their lunch break. And to be fair, I have worked in garages where that kind of thing happened. At my last shop, a few years ago, there was this one lube tech who was clearly on meth—just sweating through his coveralls in the middle of December, grinding his teeth, dropping sockets everywhere, always paranoid. 

But that is absolutely not me. I don’t touch any of that stuff. Never have. Not cocaine, not meth, not pills, not even weed or anything recreational. My husband and I are actually pretty boring when it comes to that. We might have a beer or two on a Friday night while we're watching TV, but that’s literally it. I have to be sharp for my job, you know? You can’t be messing around under a two-ton vehicle on a hydraulic lift if your head isn't completely clear. It's incredibly dangerous. One wrong move and you could crush yourself or someone else, or mess up a customer's brake lines and cause a massive wreck on the highway. So I take my sobriety really, really seriously. 

I know that hearing a voice coming out of a car manifold sounds exactly like something a person tweaking on drugs would say, I'm not stupid, I get how it sounds to you. But I promise you, I am completely sober. I haven't taken a single thing. That's why it's so terrifying to me, because I know my system is completely clean and I'm still hearing him plain as day.
Do you believe someone is actually using the vents or the cars to send you these messages?

Well, the vents... I mean, I don't know the exact physical mechanics of how he's projecting the voice through the ductwork, but I do know that it's part of something much bigger. Because it's not just the voice in the cars or the HVAC system. I know it sounds completely far-fetched, I really do, and if somebody came up to me a year ago and told me this, I would have looked at them like they had two heads. But I am absolutely convinced that my husband and the shop owner—his name is Gary, he's owned the garage for like twenty-five years—are working together to monitor me. 

They’ve been using the EV chargers and the security cameras to track exactly what I’m doing all day. We just had these new Level 3 DC fast chargers installed out in the front bays a few months ago because, you know, the market is shifting and we’re servicing a lot more electric vehicles now. They’re these heavy-duty networked stations, they have their own Wi-Fi and diagnostic uplinks, and ever since they went in, Gary is constantly in the office messing with the network. And my husband, who works in logistics and has absolutely no reason to care about automotive infrastructure, is suddenly asking all these incredibly specific questions about my bay and where I'm standing when I work. 

I know they've tapped the cameras into those charging stations to keep tabs on me. I actually confronted them about it last week. I was so fed up that I just dropped my torque wrench, marched right into the front office, and I demanded that Gary show me the security feed. And my husband actually drove down to the shop, which just proves they're coordinating this, right? Why else would he drop everything on a Tuesday afternoon to come to my work? They sat me down in the office, and they pulled up the security footage on Gary's computer monitor, and they spent an hour trying to gaslight me. They kept rewinding the footage and pointing at the screen, saying, "Look, there’s nothing there, it’s just a standard closed-circuit feed, the EV chargers don't even have cameras on them, nobody is tracking you." 

But I know what I know. You can doctor video feeds, you can hide IP addresses, you can do all sorts of things if you have the right software. So even when they show me the footage and swear up and down that there’s nothing there, I don't buy it for a second. I am still convinced they are tracking my every single move. That’s why the voice in the manifold keeps telling me not to trust my husband. It all connects back to those chargers and the cameras, I just haven't figured out exactly how they're transmitting the audio yet.
How long have you been hearing this man's voice?

Well, if I really sit down and look at the calendar, trace it all back to when I first started noticing the whispers and the weird network stuff with the chargers... it’s been about ten months now. 

Ten months of this. It started back in the late fall, right around the time we were doing a massive push on winterizations at the shop. You know, swapping out summer tires for snow tires, flushing coolant systems, checking battery loads—that whole seasonal rush where everyone suddenly panics and remembers they need their car serviced right before the first big freeze hits. We were working twelve-hour shifts, and that’s when I first heard him. And it wasn't just the voice that started then, either. That's exactly when the whole tracking situation began, too, with Gary and my husband. The voices and the tracking, it all kind of kicked off together about ten months ago.

At first, like I said, I tried to rationalize it. I’d be under a chassis on the lift, draining an oil pan, and I'd hear this faint man's voice, and I'd just tell myself, "Okay, it's just the wind whistling down the exhaust vents," or "It's just talk radio carrying from the waiting room." But then it didn't stop. It just kept going, day after day, week after week, getting louder and more specific. 

Do you have any idea how exhausting that is? Ten whole months of looking over my shoulder, checking the sightlines of the security cameras, popping a hood and having to physically brace myself because I know I'm about to hear him tell me my husband is plotting against me. I mean, ten months is a really, really long time to be on high alert every single shift. Especially when you're trying to diagnose complex engine misfires or do delicate electrical routing. You need focus for that, and for ten months my focus has been split between the cars, the vents, the cameras, and my husband's weird behavior. It's just... it's been ten months of pure exhaustion, honestly.
During these past ten months, have you had a period where you felt unusually high, energized, or irritable for days at a time?

Yeah, actually... yes. It’s like a switch flips, honestly. I’ll get into these modes where I just have this insane amount of energy, like electricity is just humming right under my skin. I’ll be flying high, totally wired, feeling like I can literally fix every single car in town. I’ll take on extra tickets, I’ll stay late, I’ll be knocking out brake jobs and timing belts like it’s nothing, just feeling completely unstoppable and brilliant, like my brain is firing on all cylinders and nobody can keep up with me. 

But then, the flip side of that is... well, my fuse gets incredibly short. Almost nonexistent. If I’m in that zone and somebody interrupts my flow, it’s bad. Like, if I get home from the shop and my husband has the nerve to ask why the dishes aren’t done, or if I'm at work and another tech just bumps my cart or moves my socket set—which, by the way, you never touch another mechanic's tools, that is rule number one in any garage, you just don't do it—but if they just move a socket even an inch, I absolutely lose it. I mean, I completely blow up. 

I start yelling at them because in that moment, it feels exactly like they’re doing it on purpose to sabotage me. It feels like they are deliberately trying to hold me down and ruin my momentum. And I know, logically, maybe it sounds like an extreme reaction to a dirty plate in the sink or a misplaced ten-millimeter socket, but when I'm running that hot, I just explode. It happens for days at a time where I'm just bouncing between feeling like an absolute genius who can overhaul an engine blindfolded, and wanting to rip someone's head off because they looked at me wrong or got in my way. It's just this intense, non-stop rush.
What is the longest that one of those high-energy, short-fuse periods has lasted without stopping?

Well, honestly, if I really sit down and think about it... they haven't really stopped. I mean, these long stretches of getting practically zero sleep, having all these racing plans constantly flooding my brain, and just being in this state of nonstop activity... that’s actually been happening for around eleven months now. 

Which is crazy to think about, because that means it started a whole month before I even noticed the tracking and the voices in the vents. I remember it perfectly because it was right at the end of August, it was still absolutely sweltering in the bays, and we had those massive industrial fans blowing just to keep us from passing out. But I wasn't tired at all. I was going home and maybe sleeping for two hours a night, tops, and I’d wake up at 3 AM feeling completely electrified. I started drawing up these incredibly detailed, color-coded schematics for reorganizing the entire parts room. I was mapping out exactly where the O-rings and the gaskets and the serpentine belts should go to optimize our workflow by like, thirty or forty percent. I brought the whole binder to Gary the next morning, and he just brushed me off, but my mind was just moving so fast, just racing with all these brilliant plans for the shop.

And it just hasn’t shut off since. Eleven months of just... go, go, go. I’ll be under a chassis, wrenching on a suspension, and my brain is already three cars ahead, diagnosing a transmission slip on the next ticket while I'm still tightening bolts on the current job. My husband keeps trying to get me to slow down, trying to make me drink sleepytime tea and telling me I need to rest, but how can I rest? How can
Have you heard the voice or felt monitored during a time when your mood was completely normal?

Well, yeah. I mean, yes, definitely. There was a time, maybe... I don't know, a couple of weeks back in the spring, where the energy kind of leveled out for a minute. It was weird because I wasn't bouncing off the walls, I wasn't drawing up any new schematics for the shop, and I was actually sleeping. Like, real sleep, maybe six or seven hours a night, which felt so strange after running on empty for so long. My husband was thrilled, of course, making me dinner and acting like everything was just fine and dandy. I wasn't snapping at people over misplaced tools, I was just going to work, turning wrenches, and coming home. My mood was completely normal, totally flat, just... regular.

But the thing is, even during those quieter weeks, the voice didn't stop. Not for a second. I'd be doing a simple brake pad replacement, feeling totally calm, and I'd still hear him coming through the exhaust vents. He was still there, clear as day, whispering about the network and the chargers. And the tracking? That didn't stop either. Even when I was getting a full night's sleep and feeling completely balanced, I still knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that Gary and my husband were monitoring me. I'd be sitting at the kitchen table, feeling totally relaxed, but I'd still be watching my husband's phone, knowing he was checking my location, knowing they were coordinating. So, yeah, even when my mood was completely fine and I wasn't making all those huge plans, all of that other stuff—the voice in the garage, the tracking—it was all still happening exactly the same as before.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when the voice and the feeling of being monitored were still there, but you were not feeling unusually high, energized, or irritable?

Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying, it was definitely at least two weeks. Honestly, it was probably closer to three weeks if I really sit down and map out the calendar. I know for a fact it was right at the end of April going into May, because we were doing our big quarterly shop inventory, which always takes a solid two and a half weeks to get through with all the parts we stock. 

And during that entire stretch, like I was telling you, I was actually sleeping. I wasn't staying up all night drafting those new workflow schematics or making those huge, elaborate plans for the bays. I wasn't snapping at the other techs or feeling that electricity under my skin. My body just felt... quiet, you know? I was getting my seven hours, drinking that sleepytime tea my husband was always pushing on me, and just doing my job. 

But even with all that quiet, even during those few weeks when my mood was totally leveled out and I wasn't running hot at all, the voice in the garage exhaust vents never took a single day off. Not once. I'd be in the back room counting boxes of oil filters and spark plugs for three hours straight, feeling totally calm, not energized or irritable in the slightest, and I'd still hear him right there in the metal, talking about the network and the chargers. 

And the tracking didn't stop either. I mean, even though I wasn't manic or whatever you want to call it, I still knew, with absolute certainty, that Gary and my husband were watching my every move. I'd be driving home from the shop, not speeding, not racing my thoughts, just cruising exactly at the speed limit, and I'd still be staring at my phone on the passenger seat because I knew they had the location pinging. I knew they were coordinating. So yes, for that solid two or three-week block, the high energy and the big plans were completely gone, but the voice and the tracking were still right there, every single day, just as intense as always.

Yeah, actually... yes. It’s like a switch flips, honestly. I’ll get into these modes where I just have this insane amount of energy, like electricity is just humming right under my skin. I’ll be flying high, totally wired, feeling like I can literally fix every single car in town. I’ll take on extra tickets, I’ll stay late, I’ll be knocking out brake jobs and timing belts like it’s nothing, just feeling completely unstoppable and brilliant, like my brain is firing on all cylinders and nobody can keep up with me. 

But then, the flip side of that is... well, my fuse gets incredibly short. Almost nonexistent. If I’m in that zone and somebody interrupts my flow, it’s bad. Like, if I get home from the shop and my husband has the nerve to ask why the dishes aren’t done, or if I'm at work and another tech just bumps my cart or moves my socket set—which, by the way, you never touch another mechanic's tools, that is rule number one in any garage, you just don't do it—but if they just move a socket even an inch, I absolutely lose it. I mean, I completely blow up. 

I start yelling at them because in that moment, it feels exactly like they’re doing it on purpose to sabotage me. It feels like they are deliberately trying to hold me down and ruin my momentum. And I know, logically, maybe it sounds like an extreme reaction to a dirty plate in the sink or a misplaced ten-millimeter socket, but when I'm running that hot, I just explode. It happens for days at a time where I'm just bouncing between feeling like an absolute genius who can overhaul an engine blindfolded, and wanting to rip someone's head off because they looked at me wrong or got in my way. It's just this intense, non-stop rush.

Well, honestly, if I really sit down and think about it... they haven't really stopped. I mean, these long stretches of getting practically zero sleep, having all these racing plans constantly flooding my brain, and just being in this state of nonstop activity... that’s actually been happening for around eleven months now. 

Which is crazy to think about, because that means it started a whole month before I even noticed the tracking and the voices in the vents. I remember it perfectly because it was right at the end of August, it was still absolutely sweltering in the bays, and we had those massive industrial fans blowing just to keep us from passing out. But I wasn't tired at all. I was going home and maybe sleeping for two hours a night, tops, and I’d wake up at 3 AM feeling completely electrified. I started drawing up these incredibly detailed, color-coded schematics for reorganizing the entire parts room. I was mapping out exactly where the O-rings and the gaskets and the serpentine belts should go to optimize our workflow by like, thirty or forty percent. I brought the whole binder to Gary the next morning, and he just brushed me off, but my mind was just moving so fast, just racing with all these brilliant plans for the shop.

And it just hasn’t shut off since. Eleven months of just... go, go, go. I’ll be under a chassis, wrenching on a suspension, and my brain is already three cars ahead, diagnosing a transmission slip on the next ticket while I'm still tightening bolts on the current job. doctor.intent: Determine whether psychotic symptoms have ever occurred outside of the prolonged elevated/irritable mood period, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you heard the voice or felt monitored during a time when your mood was completely normal?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: Even during a quieter few weeks when I was sleeping more and wasn’t making huge plans, I still heard the garage voice and believed my husband and boss were tracking me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient experienced hallucinations or delusions during a time when their mood was normal, which directly corresponds to the requirement of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah. I mean, yes, definitely. There was a time, maybe... I don't know, a couple of weeks back in the spring, where the energy kind of leveled out for a minute. It was weird because I wasn't bouncing off the walls, I wasn't drawing up any new schematics for the shop, and I was actually sleeping. Like, real sleep, maybe six or seven hours a night, which felt so strange after running on empty for so long. My husband was thrilled, of course, making me dinner and acting like everything was just fine and dandy. I wasn't snapping at people over misplaced tools, I was just going to work, turning wrenches, and coming home. My mood was completely normal, totally flat, just... regular.

But the thing is, even during those quieter weeks, the voice didn't stop. Not for a second. I'd be doing a simple brake pad replacement, feeling totally calm, and I'd still hear him coming through the exhaust vents. He was still there, clear as day, whispering about the network and the chargers. And the tracking? That didn't stop either. Even when I was getting a full night's sleep and feeling completely balanced, I still knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that Gary and my husband were monitoring me. I'd be sitting at the kitchen table, feeling totally relaxed, but I'd still be watching my husband's phone, knowing he was checking my location, knowing they were coordinating. So, yeah, even when my mood was completely fine and I wasn't making all those huge plans, all of that other stuff—the voice in the garage, the tracking—it was all still happening exactly the same as before.

inference.note: Psychosis persisted during a euthymic period, which rules out mood-congruent psychosis limited to mania and makes F25.0 more likely than F31.2. Duration and syndrome make F30.2, F29, and F06.2 less likely.

doctor.question: Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when the voice and the feeling of being monitored were still there, but you were not feeling unusually high, energized, or irritable?

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying, it was definitely at least two weeks. Honestly, it was probably closer to three weeks if I really sit down and map out the calendar. I know for a fact it was right at the end of April going into May, because we were doing our big quarterly shop inventory, which always takes a solid two and a half weeks to get through with all the parts we stock. 

And during that entire stretch, like I was telling you, I was actually sleeping. I wasn't staying up all night drafting those new workflow schematics or making those huge, elaborate plans for the bays. I wasn't snapping at the other techs or feeling that electricity under my skin. My body just felt... quiet, you know? I was getting my seven hours, drinking that sleepytime tea my husband was always pushing on me, and just doing my job. 

But even with all that quiet, even during those few weeks when my mood was totally leveled out and I wasn't running hot at all, the voice in the garage exhaust vents never took a single day off. Not once. I'd be in the back room counting boxes of oil filters and spark plugs for three hours straight, feeling totally calm, not energized or irritable in the slightest, and I'd still hear him right there in the metal, talking about the network and the chargers. 

And the tracking didn't stop either. I mean, even though I wasn't manic or whatever you want to call it, I still knew, with absolute certainty, that Gary and my husband were watching my every move. I'd be driving home from the shop, not speeding, not racing my thoughts, just cruising exactly at the speed limit, and I'd still be staring at my phone on the passenger seat because I knew they had the location pinging. I knew they were coordinating. So yes, for that solid two or three-week block, the high energy and the big plans were completely gone, but the voice and the tracking were still right there, every single day, just as intense as always.
